notes: Community pack, roadmap Phase 1 candidate. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: Drawing, colour and the seeing eye

themes.theme: Drawing what is there, not what you know
themes.description: Observation over symbol — contour, negative space and the practice of trusting the eye against the brain's shorthand.
themes.transfer_check: Produce an observational drawing of a real object using contour and negative-space methods, alongside the from-memory version that shows the difference.

bands.K–2: Draw a real object by looking at it, not by memory, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Draw a real object slowly, looking at its edges more than your paper.
bands.6–8: Draw one object using contour lines, looking more than drawing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draw a real object using contour and negative space, trusting the eye over habit.
bands.11–12: Draw a real complex object from observation alone, defending each choice against symbolic shorthand.

themes.theme: Light and the shape it makes
themes.description: Value, shadow and form — how five tones turn a circle into a sphere.
themes.transfer_check: Render one real lit object in a five-value study where the light direction is unmistakable.

bands.K–2: Shine a light on a ball and draw the dark and light parts, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Draw a round object showing where the light and shadow fall.
bands.6–8: Draw a sphere using three values of shading, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draw a real object using five tones of value to show its form.
bands.11–12: Draw a real still life using a full value range to convincingly render three-dimensional form.

themes.theme: Colour: the wheel and the why
themes.description: Hue, value, saturation and the relationships — complement, analogue, temperature — that make palettes work.
themes.transfer_check: Mix and apply a deliberate limited palette for one image, and name the relationship rule the palette obeys.

bands.K–2: Mix two paint colours together and see what happens, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Name two colours that sit opposite each other on a colour wheel.
bands.6–8: Mix a complementary colour pair and use them in a small piece, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build a real palette using complement, analogue or temperature relationships.
bands.11–12: Design and defend a real palette for a piece, using colour theory to justify each choice.

themes.description: Framing, thirds, leading lines and the deliberate placement of what matters — the picture as a directed path.
themes.transfer_check: Recompose one weak image (yours or found) two different ways and explain which compositional move fixed it.

bands.K–2: Move a picture around a page until it looks good, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Place the main thing in a drawing off to one side instead of the middle.
bands.6–8: Compose a drawing using the rule of thirds, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compose a real piece using leading lines and deliberate placement of what matters.
bands.11–12: Compose a real piece and explain the directed path you built for the viewer's eye.

themes.description: Proportion, gesture and the quick pose — drawing people as structures in motion rather than assembled features.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a set of timed gesture drawings from a live or video model, with the last showing measurably better proportion than the first.

bands.K–2: Draw a stick figure doing something active, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Draw a person in a quick pose, focused on the pose not the details.
bands.6–8: Draw three quick gesture poses in under a minute each, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draw a real figure using proportion and gesture rather than assembled features.
bands.11–12: Draw a real model or reference through multiple quick gesture studies, defending the structural choices.

themes.description: Pencil, ink, paint, digital — what each medium wants to do, and choosing the tool for the intention.
themes.transfer_check: Execute the same small subject in three media and articulate what each medium gave and refused.

bands.K–2: Try drawing with two different tools and say which you liked, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Draw the same thing with pencil and then with ink and compare.
bands.6–8: Use two materials on one subject and describe what each does differently, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Choose a real material for a piece based on what it wants to do, and defend the choice.
bands.11–12: Complete a real piece in a deliberately chosen medium, defending why that medium served the intention.

themes.description: Studying artists you love, the master copy as a tool, and the line between learning from and passing off.
themes.transfer_check: Make one labelled master copy, then one original piece applying its lesson, and state exactly what was borrowed.

bands.K–2: Look at an artist's work you like and try to draw something similar, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Copy part of a real artist's drawing as practice.
bands.6–8: Make a study copy of a real artist's work and say what you learned, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Make a real master copy as a learning tool and explain the line between learning and copying.
bands.11–12: Complete a real study in an admired artist's style and articulate where influence ends and originality begins.

themes.description: Daily pages, bad drawings on purpose, and the sketchbook as a private gym rather than a gallery.
themes.transfer_check: Keep a daily sketchbook for two weeks and present it with your own annotation of what improved and what to attack next.

bands.K–2: Draw one small thing every day for a week, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Fill one page a day in a sketchbook for a week.
bands.6–8: Fill five sketchbook pages with quick, imperfect drawings, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Keep a real sketchbook practice for two weeks, treating it as private practice not a gallery.
bands.11–12: Maintain a real sketchbook habit across a month and select one page that shows real growth.

themes.description: Describing before judging, the question behind the criticism, and hearing feedback as data rather than verdict.
themes.transfer_check: Give a structured critique of a peer's work (describe, analyse, suggest) and revise one of your own pieces from critique received.

bands.K–2: Say one thing you notice about a friend's drawing, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Describe what you see in a classmate's drawing before saying if you like it.
bands.6–8: Describe two things in a peer's work before giving an opinion, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Give a real critique that describes before it judges, and receive one as data not verdict.
bands.11–12: Lead a real critique session, describing work precisely and receiving feedback as usable data.

themes.description: When a piece is done, preparing work for a wall or a feed, and the small courage of putting it where people look.
themes.transfer_check: Finish, title and publicly display one work — physical or online — and document one response you received.

bands.K–2: Decide a drawing is done and show it to someone, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Pick your best drawing from the week and show it to someone.
bands.6–8: Prepare one finished piece to display, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Prepare a real piece for a wall or feed, deciding when it is truly finished.
bands.11–12: Prepare and present a real finished body of work publicly, defending the decision to show it.

themes.description: Active listening — picking out instruments, structure and production choices instead of letting music be wallpaper.
themes.transfer_check: Map one song's full structure and instrumentation from listening alone, verified against a second listener or source.

bands.K–2: Listen to a song with an adult and point out the drums.
bands.3–5: Listen to a song and name two instruments you hear.
bands.6–8: Listen to a song and identify its structure — verse and chorus, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Listen actively to a real song and identify instruments, structure and one production choice.
bands.11–12: Analyse a real song's structure and production choices in a written or spoken breakdown.

themes.theme: Pulse, rhythm and the body's clock
themes.description: Beat, subdivision and groove — internalising time before any instrument is touched.
themes.transfer_check: Clap or play three distinct rhythm patterns against a steady beat, holding each through a distraction.

bands.K–2: Clap along to a steady beat with an adult.
bands.3–5: Clap a steady beat all the way through while a song plays.
bands.6–8: Clap a beat and its subdivision for one song, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Internalise a real song's pulse and subdivision without an instrument, then clap it exactly.
bands.11–12: Demonstrate real rhythmic internalisation across a complex groove, teaching it to a peer.

themes.description: Matching pitch, carrying a melody, and why 'tone deaf' is almost always untrained rather than untrue.
themes.transfer_check: Sing or play back a short unfamiliar melody accurately after limited hearings, alone or in unison.

bands.K–2: Sing a note back to an adult as closely as you can.
bands.3–5: Sing a short simple tune back after hearing it once.
bands.6–8: Match pitch on five notes and carry a short melody, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Match pitch reliably and carry a real melody, understanding why 'tone deaf' is usually untrained.
bands.11–12: Train and demonstrate reliable pitch-matching across a real range, teaching the skill to someone unconfident.

themes.theme: Harmony: notes that agree and argue
themes.description: Chords, progressions and the four chords under half the songs you know.
themes.transfer_check: Play or program a common progression and identify it by ear inside two real songs.

bands.K–2: Play two notes together and say if they sound nice or strange, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Tell apart a chord that sounds finished from one that sounds unfinished.
bands.6–8: Play a simple chord progression and name one chord, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Play a real chord progression and identify the four chords under half the songs you know.
bands.11–12: Play and analyse a real progression, explaining the tension and resolution it creates.

themes.description: Posture, tone production and the practice loop — beginning an instrument with habits that will not need undoing.
themes.transfer_check: Perform a simple piece on your instrument with assessed posture and tone, plus your practice log for the fortnight behind it.

bands.K–2: Hold a real instrument correctly with an adult and make one clean sound.
bands.3–5: Play three clean notes on a real instrument with correct posture.
bands.6–8: Play ten notes with correct posture and tone, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Play a real instrument's first exercises with habits that will not need undoing later.
bands.11–12: Demonstrate a real instrument's fundamentals to a beginner, modelling posture and tone from the start.

themes.theme: Reading and the other ways in
themes.description: Notation, tab, chord charts and ear — the entry systems into written music and when each serves.
themes.transfer_check: Learn one short piece from written form (notation, tab or chart) without a recording, then verify against one.

bands.K–2: Follow along with a simple picture of a song while it plays, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Follow along on a chord chart while a friend plays one song.
bands.6–8: Read a simple chart or tab and play along, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real chart, tab or ear-based system and say when each serves best.
bands.11–12: Compare real entry systems into music — notation, tab, ear — and use each to learn the same piece.

themes.description: Ensemble craft: listening across, entering together, and the discipline of being quiet enough.
themes.transfer_check: Rehearse and perform one piece with at least one other musician, holding your part against theirs.

bands.K–2: Play one note when it is your turn with a friend, in time.
bands.3–5: Play a simple part with a partner, staying in time together.
bands.6–8: Play a part with a partner, entering together and leaving space, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Play in a real ensemble, entering together and being quiet enough to hear others.
bands.11–12: Perform in a real ensemble, demonstrating listening-across and disciplined entrances and space.

themes.theme: Making a track in the box
themes.description: Loops, layers, arrangement — producing a piece of music in software from silence to bounce.
themes.transfer_check: Produce and export a one-minute original track with at least four intentional layers, and walk through your arrangement choices.

bands.K–2: Add one sound to a simple music app with an adult.
bands.3–5: Layer two sounds in a music app to make something new.
bands.6–8: Layer loops into a short arrangement using software, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce a real short piece in software from loops to a finished bounce.
bands.11–12: Produce a real original arrangement in software, from silence to finished mixdown.

themes.theme: The song: words that are music
themes.description: Lyric, hook and form — writing a song that says one thing and lands it.
themes.transfer_check: Write and perform (or demo) one original song with a defined hook, and state the single thing it says.

bands.K–2: Make up a short rhyme about your day with an adult.
bands.3–5: Write two lines that say one thing clearly.
bands.6–8: Write a short song section with a hook and one clear idea, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a real song with lyric, hook and form that says one thing and lands it.
bands.11–12: Write and perform a real complete song, defending that it says one thing and lands it.

themes.description: Traditions, borrowings and the histories inside genres — listening to music as the record of the people who made it.
themes.transfer_check: Trace one genre you enjoy back through two of its source traditions with listening examples, and present the chain.

bands.K–2: Say what kind of music your family likes, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Name one music tradition and one thing you know about it.
bands.6–8: Name two music traditions and one thing each borrowed from, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Research a real genre's history and one thing it borrowed from another tradition.
bands.11–12: Present a real genre's cultural history, tracing its borrowings and the people who made it.

themes.description: What is in, what is out, and where the camera stands — every shot as a decision about what the viewer may know.
themes.transfer_check: Photograph one subject five ways — distance, angle, framing — and explain what each frame lets the viewer believe.

bands.K–2: Take a photo of something and say why you chose what is in it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Take two photos of the same thing framed differently and compare.
bands.6–8: Take three photos with different framing and explain one choice, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Shoot a real scene with deliberate framing choices, explaining what each excludes.
bands.11–12: Shoot and defend a real sequence's framing, explaining what each shot lets the viewer know.

themes.description: Finding, shaping and waiting for light — why the hour and the window beat the expensive camera.
themes.transfer_check: Shoot the same subject in three different lighting conditions and rank the results with the reasons visible in the images.

bands.K–2: Take a photo near a window and one far from it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Take two photos in different light and say which looks better.
bands.6–8: Shoot the same subject in two light sources and compare, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Shoot a real subject using available light well, without relying on an expensive camera.
bands.11–12: Shoot and light a real subject deliberately, defending the choice of hour and window over gear.

themes.description: Why audiences forgive bad video and abandon bad audio — mic placement, room noise and the recorded room tone.
themes.transfer_check: Record the same short scene with camera audio and with a placed microphone, and present the difference.

bands.K–2: Record your voice and say if it sounds clear, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Record a short video and say if the sound is clear.
bands.6–8: Record with attention to mic placement and check room noise, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Record real audio with correct mic placement and manage room noise and tone.
bands.11–12: Record and clean real audio for a project, defending choices that audiences forgive video for but not sound.

themes.description: Questions that open people, listening while operating, and the ethics of what your subject didn't realise they said.
themes.transfer_check: Record a five-minute interview with a real subject — framed, lit, mic'd — and cut its best two minutes honestly.

bands.K–2: Ask a grown-up one question and listen to their answer, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Ask someone three questions and listen without interrupting.
bands.6–8: Ask five open questions and listen while operating a camera, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Conduct a real interview with open questions, listening well while recording.
bands.11–12: Conduct and edit a real interview, handling the ethics of what a subject did not realise they said.

themes.description: Selection, order and rhythm — how meaning is made in the cut, and made differently by a different cut.
themes.transfer_check: Cut the same footage into two versions with different meanings or moods, and screen both.

bands.K–2: Pick your favourite of two video clips to show, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Choose which of three clips to use and in what order.
bands.6–8: Edit three clips into an order that tells a small story, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Edit real footage, choosing selection, order and rhythm to make meaning.
bands.11–12: Edit a real project two different ways and explain how the cut changed the meaning.

themes.description: Short-form structure: hook, turn, payoff — the discipline of a complete story inside a feed's attention span.
themes.transfer_check: Make a ninety-second piece with an identifiable hook, turn and payoff, and test it on a viewer who owes you nothing.

bands.K–2: Tell a very short story in three sentences, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Tell a story in under a minute with a beginning, middle and end.
bands.6–8: Structure a ninety-second story with a hook, a turn and a payoff, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Edit a real ninety-second story with hook, turn and payoff inside the attention span.
bands.11–12: Produce a real short-form piece to a strict time limit, defending the discipline of the cut.

themes.description: Staging, cropping, colour and AI generation — where enhancement ends and deception begins, and the disclosure that keeps trust.
themes.transfer_check: Take one of your own images or clips, push it past the honest line deliberately, and mark the exact edit where it stopped being true.

bands.K–2: Say if a photo looks real or changed, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Spot one way a photo might be changed from the original.
bands.6–8: Compare an edited and unedited photo and say what changed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify real edits, staging or generation in an image and where enhancement becomes deception.
bands.11–12: Analyse a real edited image's ethics and write the disclosure that would keep trust.

themes.theme: Faces, consent and the right to be unfilmed
themes.description: Filming people: consent, minors, public space law and the human ask behind the legal minimum.
themes.transfer_check: Produce a short piece involving other people with documented consent, and state where law and courtesy diverged.

bands.K–2: Ask before taking a picture of someone, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Ask permission before filming a friend and respect a no.
bands.6–8: Get consent from two people before filming them, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Get real informed consent before filming real people, including a minor's guardian.
bands.11–12: Handle a real filming consent scenario correctly, including public space law and a person's right to refuse.

themes.description: Formats, thumbnails, captions and what each platform's machine rewards — distributing work without being distributed by it.
themes.transfer_check: Publish one piece properly prepared for two different platforms, and compare what each did to it and for it.

bands.K–2: Show your video to a friend and see if they like it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Post a short video and see what makes people watch it.
bands.6–8: Format one video for a platform with a thumbnail and caption, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Format a real video for a platform, choosing what its algorithm rewards without being ruled by it.
bands.11–12: Publish a real project across a platform's format constraints while defending your own creative intent.

themes.description: Projects over posts: series, consistency and the portfolio that shows a maker rather than a lucky upload.
themes.transfer_check: Plan and complete a three-piece series with a stated through-line, presented as a single body of work.

bands.K–2: Make three small pictures that go together, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Make three short videos on the same idea.
bands.6–8: Make a small series of three related pieces, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build a real short series showing consistency of subject or style.
bands.11–12: Assemble a real portfolio of consistent work that shows a maker rather than one lucky upload.

tracks.name: The stage and the spoken word

themes.description: Stance, stillness, breath and the eyes — occupying a space before saying anything in it.
themes.transfer_check: Hold a stage or room entrance, pause and first line before an audience, with feedback on presence alone.

bands.K–2: Stand still and take a breath before speaking to a group, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Stand quietly for five seconds before starting to speak.
bands.6–8: Stand still, breathe and hold the room for five seconds before speaking, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Occupy a real space with stillness and breath before saying anything.
bands.11–12: Command a real stage's stillness and presence before a word is spoken, assessed on the hold.

themes.theme: The voice that reaches the back
themes.description: Breath support, projection, pace and the pause — a voice that carries without shouting.
themes.transfer_check: Deliver the same passage to the back of a real room quietly failing and then correctly projecting, confirmed by a listener there.

bands.K–2: Say a word loudly enough for someone across the room to hear, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Project your voice to reach the back of a room.
bands.6–8: Project a short line to reach the back of a room without shouting, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Project a real line with breath support, pace and a pause, reaching the back of a real room.
bands.11–12: Deliver a real speech projecting to a full room, using pace and pause deliberately.

themes.theme: Saying words you did not write
themes.description: Text work: meaning first, memory second, and making a written line sound like it occurred to you.
themes.transfer_check: Perform a memorised minute of someone else's text with intention choices you can defend line by line.

bands.K–2: Say a line from a book as if you meant it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Memorise and say a short line someone else wrote.
bands.6–8: Perform a memorised line so it sounds like it occurred to you, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Perform a real memorised text with meaning first, sounding natural rather than recited.
bands.11–12: Perform a real scripted monologue, defending the choices that made someone else's words your own.

themes.description: Accepting offers, building with a partner and failing cheerfully in public — improvisation as trained generosity.
themes.transfer_check: Play three improv structures with a partner before observers, sustaining accept-and-build throughout.

bands.K–2: Add one idea to a friend's pretend game, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Build on a partner's idea in a made-up scene.
bands.6–8: Accept and build on a partner's offer in a short improvised scene, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Improvise a real scene, accepting offers and building generously with a partner.
bands.11–12: Perform real improvisation, failing cheerfully in public and building trust with a partner live.

themes.theme: The character who is not you
themes.description: Body, voice, want — building someone else from observable choices rather than costume.
themes.transfer_check: Present the same short scene as two distinct characters, changed by observable physical and vocal choices only.

bands.K–2: Pretend to be someone else for a minute, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Play a character different from yourself for a short scene.
bands.6–8: Build a character's body and voice for one short scene, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build a real character from observable choices — body, voice, want — not costume.
bands.11–12: Perform a real character built from specific choices, defending them as more than costume.

themes.theme: The speech with a job to do
themes.description: Persuading, honouring, explaining — occasion speeches structured for their actual purpose and audience.
themes.transfer_check: Write and deliver a three-minute speech for a real occasion and purpose, judged against whether it did its job.

bands.K–2: Say why you like something to a group, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Give a short speech about why something matters to you.
bands.6–8: Give a short speech structured to persuade or explain, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Structure and deliver a real occasion speech for its actual purpose and audience.
bands.11–12: Deliver a real occasion speech — persuading, honouring, explaining — structured for its true purpose.

themes.description: What stage fright is physiologically, the preparation that shrinks it, and performing well while still afraid.
themes.transfer_check: Perform after deliberately rehearsing a personal pre-performance routine, and report what the nerves did and what you did back.

bands.K–2: Say you feel nervous before speaking, and take a breath, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Notice what your body does when you are nervous to speak.
bands.6–8: Name what stage fright feels like and one thing that shrinks it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Prepare for real stage fright and perform well while still feeling it.
bands.11–12: Perform a real piece while managing real nerves, and explain the preparation that shrank them.

themes.description: Rehearsal discipline, hitting cues, and the offstage professionalism that companies are actually built on.
themes.transfer_check: Rehearse and perform a group piece hitting every entrance and cue, with the stage manager's log as evidence.

bands.K–2: Wait for your turn to speak in a group activity, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Hit your cue to speak or move in a group scene.
bands.6–8: Hit two cues correctly in a rehearsed scene, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Hit real cues reliably in rehearsal, building the offstage discipline companies run on.
bands.11–12: Rehearse and perform in a real ensemble, demonstrating the professionalism that holds a company together.

themes.theme: The audience is part of the show
themes.description: Reading a room, riding laughter and silence, and recovering the moment that just died.
themes.transfer_check: Perform one piece twice for different audiences and describe, specifically, what you adjusted between them and why.

bands.K–2: Notice if people are laughing or quiet during a performance, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Notice how an audience reacts and adjust your pace.
bands.6–8: Read an audience's laughter or silence and adjust once, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real audience and recover a moment that went quiet or died.
bands.11–12: Read and steer a real audience through a full performance, recovering a real dead moment live.

themes.description: The production itself: space, tickets, tech, front of house — the unglamorous machine around every performance.
themes.transfer_check: Take one named production role (stage manager, tech, producer, FOH) through a real event and deliver its checklist complete.

bands.K–2: Help set up chairs or props before a show, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Help set up one part of a performance space.
bands.6–8: Set up space, props and a simple ticket system for one show, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run real front-of-house, tech and space logistics for a small performance.
bands.11–12: Produce a real show's full unglamorous machine — space, tickets, tech, front of house.

tracks.name: Craft, design and the made object

themes.description: Users, constraints and the brief — design as solving a person's problem rather than decorating your own.
themes.transfer_check: Write a real design brief from interviewing an actual user, with constraints and success criteria they confirm.

bands.K–2: Make something for a friend based on what they like, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Design something simple for another person's actual need.
bands.6–8: Design one object for a stated user need, not your own preference, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a real object for a real user's constraint, solving their problem not decorating your own.
bands.11–12: Design and defend a real object against a real brief and a real user's constraints.

themes.description: Many cheap versions before one dear one — ideation as volume, and the courage to bin the favourite.
themes.transfer_check: Produce ten distinct concept sketches for one brief, and defend which two advance and why the favourite died.

bands.K–2: Draw three quick versions of an idea and pick one, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Draw five quick versions of one idea before choosing.
bands.6–8: Sketch five cheap versions of an idea and discard four, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Iterate many cheap versions of a real design and discard the favourite if it is not the best.
bands.11–12: Run a real iterative design process, defending why the discarded favourite lost to the chosen one.

themes.theme: Materials: what wants to be what
themes.description: Wood, fabric, clay, paper, plastic — properties, joins and the material honestly matched to the job.
themes.transfer_check: Choose and justify materials for one real object, and demonstrate the appropriate joining technique for your choice.

bands.K–2: Feel two materials and say which is bendier, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Compare two materials and say which suits a small project better.
bands.6–8: Choose the right material for one small build and say why, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Choose a real material honestly matched to a job, considering its properties and joins.
bands.11–12: Choose and defend a real material against its properties, joins and the job it must do.

themes.description: Marking out, tolerances and the accumulating error — precision as respect for the future assembler and user.
themes.transfer_check: Make a multi-part object where the parts actually fit, with your marking-out shown and measured against tolerance.

bands.K–2: Measure something twice before cutting it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Measure a piece twice and mark it before cutting.
bands.6–8: Measure and mark a piece to a stated tolerance, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Mark out a real piece to a tight tolerance, understanding accumulating error.
bands.11–12: Mark and cut a real assembly to a tolerance respectful of whoever assembles it next.

themes.theme: The tool and the respect it demands
themes.description: Hand and power tools: capability, technique and the safety rules written in other people's scars.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate safe, correct technique on three tools appropriate to your level, including one you were newly trained on.

bands.K–2: Use a safe tool carefully with an adult watching.
bands.3–5: Use a hand tool correctly and put it away safely.
bands.6–8: Use two hand tools correctly and safely, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Use a real hand or power tool with correct technique and safety awareness.
bands.11–12: Demonstrate real tool competence and safety discipline, explaining the rules written in others' scars.

themes.theme: Type, layout and the designed page
themes.description: Graphic design's core: hierarchy, alignment, contrast, whitespace — making information look like what it means.
themes.transfer_check: Redesign one genuinely bad real-world document or poster, and annotate each change with the principle it applies.

bands.K–2: Arrange words and a picture on a page so it looks tidy, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Arrange text and images on a page with clear hierarchy.
bands.6–8: Design a simple page using alignment and whitespace, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a real page using hierarchy, alignment, contrast and whitespace.
bands.11–12: Design a real page that makes information look like what it means, defended against a critique.

themes.theme: The prototype that answers a question
themes.description: Building the cheapest thing that tests the riskiest assumption — prototyping as inquiry, not miniature manufacture.
themes.transfer_check: State one design's riskiest assumption, build the minimum prototype that tests it, and report the answer.

bands.K–2: Build a quick, rough version of an idea to test it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Build a cheap test version of an idea before the real one.
bands.6–8: Build a cheap prototype testing one risky assumption, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build a real cheap prototype that tests the riskiest assumption in a design.
bands.11–12: Build and test a real prototype as inquiry, defending what question it answered.

themes.description: Modifying and mending the made world — the confidence to open, alter and improve objects you own.
themes.transfer_check: Repair or usefully modify one real broken or inadequate object, documenting before, process and after.

bands.K–2: Fix something small that is broken, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Fix or improve something you own without an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Repair or modify one real object you own, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Repair or adapt a real object confidently, opening it to understand it first.
bands.11–12: Repair or significantly modify a real object, documenting the process and the improvement.

themes.description: Why some objects delight and others infuriate — analysing the designed world's hits and crimes.
themes.transfer_check: Analyse one excellent and one terrible everyday object, and specify the design decisions responsible for each.

bands.K–2: Say why you like or dislike an everyday object, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Name one object that is easy to use and one that is annoying.
bands.6–8: Analyse two designed objects for what works and what fails, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Analyse a real designed object's hits and crimes with specific reasoning.
bands.11–12: Write a real critique of a designed object's success and failure, grounded in design principles.

themes.theme: Making for someone, start to finish
themes.description: The commission: brief, design, make, deliver — one complete arc ending in an object in its user's hands.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a real commission for a real person from brief to handover, with their assessment of it against the brief.

bands.K–2: Make something for someone and give it to them, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Make a small object for a specific person's request.
bands.6–8: Take a brief, design and make one object for a real person, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Complete a real commission from brief through delivery for an actual user.
bands.11–12: Complete a real commission end to end — brief, design, make, deliver — to a real client's satisfaction.
